stories.title: Salesforce Acquires Cresta for ~$2.7B to Add Voice AI to Agentforce and Service Cloud
stories.body: On November 2, 2026, Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire Cresta, a Stanford AI Lab spinout whose voice agents resolve complex customer calls end-to-end and provide real-time guidance to human representatives. The deal — Salesforce's third CX acquisition in two weeks after its $3.6B Fin (formerly Intercom) pickup — folds Cresta into Service Cloud and Agentforce, with named enterprise customers including Marriott, Comcast, and Alaska Airlines. Cresta will continue supporting the third-party contact center and telephony platforms its customers use today, a pledge that puts Salesforce in direct competition with contact center platform vendors that are also its partners.
stories.why: Salesforce now controls Fin (chat/messaging agent), Cresta (voice agent), and Agentforce (workflow agent) — a full-stack CX suite that independent agent vendors like Sierra and Decagon will be compared against on every enterprise deal. A Graas seller must be able to articulate what differentiated, non-Salesforce-locked agent infrastructure looks like before this suite narrative dominates the conversation.

stories.title: Sierra Raises $1.75B at $30B Valuation as ARR Tops $400M, Serving Nearly Half of Fortune 50
stories.body: On November 23, 2026, Sierra Technologies — the enterprise customer-experience agent platform co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor — closed a $1.75 billion Series F, its third raise in 14 months, valuing the company at $30 billion. Sierra's annualized revenue topped $400 million in the weeks before the round closed, and the company now reports serving nearly 50% of Fortune 50 firms. Sierra powers customer agents across more than a dozen LLMs and also acquired browser-agent navigation startup Anon in November 2026 to extend its capabilities.
stories.why: Sierra is the most direct named-vendor competitor an enterprise retail prospect will reference on any AI customer-service deal — its scale ($400M ARR, Fortune 50 penetration) and outcome-based pricing model set the benchmark buyers will use to evaluate Graas. Understanding Sierra's architecture (no published rate card, custom-quoted, multi-LLM) helps sellers frame differentiated positioning around data grounding and retail-specific context layers.

stories.title: McKinsey State of AI 2026: 40% of Large Enterprises Now Scaling Agents, But Only 6% Show EBIT Impact
stories.body: McKinsey's State of AI: Global Survey 2026 — fielded May–June 2026 across 1,719 respondents in 97 countries — found that 40% of respondents from organizations with annual revenues above $1 billion report scaling AI agents, up from 27% the prior year. Despite this acceleration, the share of organizations attributing any EBIT impact to AI held flat at 37%, and high performers (those attributing 5%+ of EBIT to AI) remained at just 6%. In consumer goods and retail specifically, McKinsey found agents are most often deployed in marketing and sales activities, not supply chain or operations.
stories.why: The gap between agent deployment (40% scaling) and proven EBIT impact (6% high performers) is the exact 'pilot trap' Graas can help retail clients escape — by ensuring agents are grounded in governed, retail-specific context layers before they scale. This data gives sellers a credible third-party anchor to open the data-readiness conversation with a CIO or CDO.

stories.title: Gartner + Deloitte: Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by 2027 Due to Data Architecture Failures
stories.body: Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, with legacy system integration and data architecture constraints cited as the primary reasons — not agent capability gaps. Deloitte's 2026 Tech Trends report corroborates this, noting that most enterprise agents still rely on conventional ETL pipelines and data warehouses that create structural friction for autonomous workflows. Gartner separately forecasts that 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data will be abandoned, and that 63% of organizations either lack or are unsure they have the right data management practices for AI.
stories.why: This is the single most powerful proof point for why the data and context foundation must come before the agent — and it comes from Gartner and Deloitte, not a vendor. A Graas seller can cite this directly to explain why retail AI pilots stall and why a governed semantic/context layer is not optional infrastructure but the prerequisite for any agent deployment that survives contact with production.

stories.title: McKinsey 2026: One-Third of Enterprises Canceled a Software Purchase to Build It With Agentic Coding Tools
stories.body: McKinsey's State of AI 2026 survey found that 32% of organizations have decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build the functionality in-house using agentic coding tools — rising to nearly half among McKinsey's identified AI high-performers and 41% among technology-sector firms. The survey of 1,719 business leaders across 97 countries was published August 25, 2026. McKinsey's own data also shows one in five organizations is already constrained by AI operating costs, and that the 32% figure represents a decision not to buy — not a system in production.
stories.why: This build-vs-buy shift is the objection Graas sellers will face most often from technically sophisticated enterprise retail buyers who believe agentic coding tools let them replicate any point solution. The counter-argument lives in the McKinsey data itself: skipping a purchase is not the same as delivering ROI, and organizations without the governance maturity to maintain what they build face hidden run costs that erase the savings.
